instagram_caption:
🚀 The live-service space race: Fortnite quietly left PUBG in the dust—here’s how the numbers move.

Picture 2017. Battle royale is exploding—but it’s still “episodes,” not “a lifestyle.” In our timeline, Fortnite starts at about 85M monthly active users. PUBG is right there with ~50M. Both look like they’re set up for the long haul… and then the charts start telling a different story.

By 2019, Fortnite’s strategy clicks: constant updates, big seasonal moments, and an ecosystem that feels bigger than the game itself. Fortnite rockets from ~100M (2018) to ~170M. PUBG slips from ~85M peak energy down to ~70M—same genre, different momentum. It’s the first clear signal that “content cadence” is the real weapon.

Then 2020 hits: Fortnite becomes a cultural default. The monthly active user line jumps to ~250M. Meanwhile PUBG stays stuck around ~65M—no dramatic collapse like a crash, but a slow drain where players keep moving on to what feels fresh every week. This is the turning point where Fortnite stops competing on match quality and starts winning on routine.

From 2021 onward, the entire gaming ecosystem shifts toward creator-driven worlds. Fortnite climbs to ~320M in 2021, ~370M by 2022, and stays elite even when the category cools. PUBG keeps bleeding: ~55M (2021) to ~45M (2022), ~40M (2023), ~38M (2024), ~35M (2025).

And look at the pressure from Roblox and Minecraft: they’re also teaching players to live inside ongoing worlds. Roblox rises ~55M → ~205M. Minecraft grows ~110M → ~235M. Fortnite’s win isn’t isolated—it’s part of the “always-on” shift.

facebook_caption:
A striking timeline comparison shows how Fortnite’s live-service model evolved into an “always-on” platform—while PUBG’s audience steadily declined as player expectations shifted.

In 2017, Fortnite began with roughly 85M monthly active users (MAUs). PUBG started far lower at about 50M MAUs. Through 2018, Fortnite expanded to ~100M, while PUBG rose to ~85M, peaking near the late-2010s battle royale wave.

The decisive shift appears in 2019–2020. Fortnite climbs to ~170M MAUs in 2019 and surges to ~250M in 2020, coinciding with Epic’s increasingly frequent event cadence and its ability to turn updates into recurring “reasons to log in.” During the same period, PUBG flattens around ~70M in 2019 and ~65M in 2020—remaining relevant but losing category momentum.

From 2021 onward, PUBG’s decline becomes persistent: ~55M (2021) to ~45M (2022) to ~40M (2023) to ~38M (2024), ending around ~35M in 2025. Meanwhile, Fortnite strengthens its leadership trajectory (about ~320M in 2021, ~370M in 2022, and ~410M by 2025). The broader “ongoing world” pressure is visible too: Roblox grows from ~55M (2017) to ~205M (2025), and Minecraft from ~110M to ~235M.

Bottom line: player routine beats one-time hype. The winners build a daily habit with continuous content and community gravity.

In 2017 Fortnite is ~85M MAUs. PUBG is ~50M. Fast forward: Fortnite hits ~250M in 2020 and keeps climbing (about ~410M by 2025). PUBG? It trends down every year: ~85M (2018) → ~35M (2025).

And while Fortnite is doing its thing, Roblox and Minecraft are also rising—Roblox goes ~55M → ~205M, Minecraft ~110M → ~235M.

So what’s the lesson: it’s not just competition inside battle royale—it’s competition for your time.
